newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB's Gehrig sees Swiss inflation risk low.
newsitem.headline: SNB's Gehrig sees Swiss inflation risk low.

text.p: Swiss National Bank board member Bruno Gehrig said that Switzerland's inflation risk is currently low.
In an interview published Monday in the Swiss daily newspaper "Der Bund," he said the Swiss franc is at more "realistic" levels than it was last summer.

Asked about prospects for further easing by the SNB, he said one should "never say never" with respect to further interest rate cuts. But he also said that an excessively expansive monetary policy could lead to problems two or three years down the road.
"I am convinced that the risk of inflation at the current time is very slight," Gehrig said.
Swiss industry was currently producing below capacity, and the Swiss real estate market remained depressed.
In addition, he noted that bank lending was stagnant and global competition was keeping prices low.

With respect to the Swiss franc, Gehrig said: "I think the franc is valued more realistically and reasonably than it was last summer. This has improved the basis for a recovery. But as to where the proper franc rate is, that is something which ultimately markets must decide."
Gehrig described the SNB's current policy as being "on a middle path between too-expansive and too-restrictive."
Asked if the SNB might consider further easing, he said that "one must act according to the situation."
But he noted that monetary policy was no substitute for changes in structural policy.
"An excessive easing -- in the hope that one could wipe out the structural problems -- would exact a high toll two or three years later," Gehrig said.
Asked if the SNB would consider cutting its discount rate, now at 1.00 percent, Gehrig said this was not something the SNB was directly discussing but did not it rule out entirely.
"With respect to our policy in the coming months, we will act according to the situation, and I would not say 'no' a priori. It would not be wise to eliminate any options in advance," Gehrig said.
He also said that factors were favourable for a slight improvement in the Swiss economy in 1997.
Official forecasts are for the Swiss gross domestic product to grow by 0.5 percent in 1997, compared with a forecast decline of 0.7 percent in 1996.
